fix.summary: Seven of the eight findings are fixed and proved through the real HTTP entry points; authn-authz-06 is blocked because all four affected controllers are outside my file set (the audit named three — I found a fourth, POST /t/:slug/demo/books). Highlights: logout now revokes server-side via a per-SESSION `sid` denylist checked in SessionMiddleware (one choke point ahead of BOTH AuthGuard and TenantGuard, since tenant.guard.ts is not mine to edit), with a durable `sessionsValidAfter` fallback when the Redis write fails so a logout is never a silent no-op; a new POST /auth/sessions/revoke-all. The impersonation middleware now joins adminUser and enforces the same three columns AdminAuthGuard does, and CLOSES the support-session row on refusal. complete-setup requires a genuinely new password (required DTO field + service check + refusal to re-submit the temp one). change-email requires the current password, pins the prior address into the token, bumps sessionsValidAfter on apply, and — because EMAIL_DRIVER is console — writes the notice to the LIBRARY's own audit log (Settings → Activity) as well as the outbox. Admin MFA replacement requires password + a live code from the factor being replaced, is recorded in the admin audit log, and re-mints the caller's cookie so the sessionsValidAfter bump doesn't sign them out. Recovery codes exist and are wired into admin login. The tenant lockout now has a real DB backstop that engages exactly when Redis (and therefore the rate limiter) fails open. I also took the deeper repair the brief offered: roles.guard.ts:41's blanket `if (req.impersonation) return true` is gone, replaced by a fixed effective role ('admin') judged by the same roles.includes() expression as a signed-in user — so a future @Roles('owner') route is refused to support on the day it is written.

findings_addressed.what_changed: Added an immutable per-SESSION `sid` claim to the tenant JWT (jwt-session.service.ts), minted once per login and carried unchanged through every sliding re-issue — deliberately NOT a per-token jti, because a jti refreshed on each slide lets the browser's copy and a thief's copy drift apart so revoking one leaves the other alive. New SessionRevocationService denylists `session:revoked:<sid>` in Redis with a TTL computed to the ABSOLUTE lifetime cap (ist + SESSION_ABSOLUTE_MAX_TTL_SEC), not the current token's exp, because sliding keeps pushing exp forward. If the Redis write fails it escalates to the durable account-wide `sessionsValidAfter` bump and logs at error — a logout that reports success while recording nothing is the original defect with extra steps. The denylist is consulted in SessionMiddleware, not in a guard: platform routes use AuthGuard and tenant data routes use TenantGuard, tenant.guard.ts is outside my file set, and the middleware is the one point every request already passes, so a denylisted sid simply never becomes a req.session and both guards 401 it. Added POST /auth/sessions/revoke-all (bumps sessionsValidAfter + drops the auth cache + clears the cookie).
findings_addressed.residual_risk: The denylist read fails OPEN during a Redis outage (refusing every request would sign out every library on the platform). Bounded: a logout performed DURING the outage lands in Postgres via the fallback, and the fail-open is logged at error, throttled to once a minute. A Redis flush also drops denylist entries for sessions logged out BEFORE the flush. No UI control for "sign out everywhere" — apps/web is out of scope.

findings_addressed.what_changed: ImpersonationMiddleware now joins the adminUser into the same supportSession query (`admin: { select: { status, disabledAt, sessionsValidAfter } }`, one round-trip) and refuses to attach req.impersonation when the admin is not entitled. The decision lives in an exported pure function `adminRevocationReason()` that mirrors AdminAuthGuard's checks one-for-one and in the same order, so the two surfaces cannot drift; AdminAuthGuard now carries a comment pointing at it. On refusal the support-session row is also CLOSED (endedAt + endedReason 'admin_ended') so the library's support view stops showing an open window nobody can use.
findings_addressed.residual_risk: There is no in-app admin disable/lock endpoint to hook (AdminAuthGuard's own comment says admins are seed-managed; scripts/bootstrap-admin.ts is out of scope), so the row is closed on the offboarded admin's NEXT request rather than at the moment of the disable. If they never send another request the row stays open until its TTL — but access is already denied, and the library's kill switch still works.

findings_addressed.what_changed: No code change — all affected controllers are outside my file set. I did answer the brief's question: three is NOT all. A static scan of every mutating handler on a `t/:slug/*` route with no @Roles/@StaffWrite metadata returns EIGHT handlers, of which FOUR are genuine defects. The audit's three (members/photos.controller.ts:37+:83, catalog/covers.controller.ts:37+:87, storage/storage-demo.controller.ts:80) plus a fourth the audit missed: POST /t/:slug/demo/books (plans/plan-demo.controller.ts:122), which creates a real `Book` row in the tenant DB behind @UseGuards(TenantGuard) alone — so a volunteer can create catalogue records and burn the max_books quota, bypassing the @StaffWrite() on the real catalog controller. The remaining two hits (announcements/tenant-announcements.controller.ts:48 and :62, dismiss/ack) are NOT defects: both are scoped to session.sub, i.e. a user acknowledging their own banner, which is correct without a role guard.
findings_addressed.residual_risk: Fully open. Exact fix for each: add RolesGuard to the handler's @UseGuards and annotate @StaffWrite(). storage-demo.controller.ts already imports RolesGuard/Roles for its DELETE at :127, so that one is two tokens.

findings_addressed.what_changed: CompleteSetupDto.newPassword is now REQUIRED (@IsString + @Length(12,200)) rather than @IsOptional — a required parameter, not an optional one with a check a future caller can forget. LoginService.completeSetup takes `newPassword: string` (required in the type), rejects an empty/whitespace value, and only clears `mustChangeCredentials` inside the same write that stores the new hash and stamps sessionsValidAfter. It additionally refuses re-submitting the CURRENT password (bcrypt-compared against the stored hash): clearing the gate while the admin-known temporary credential keeps working is the exact harm of the finding. Both refusals carry machine `code`s (auth.passwordRequired / auth.passwordUnchanged) so the web can localise them. Locale strings corrected in el+en: firstLogin.subtitle and firstLogin.pwHint no longer say 'leave blank to keep your current password', and firstLogin.pwTooShort now says 12, not 4.
findings_addressed.residual_risk: apps/web/.../FirstLoginSetup.tsx still validates `password.length < 4` client-side and treats the field as optional, so a blank or short password now round-trips to a server 400 instead of being caught in the form. Degraded UX, not a hole. Also needs errors.api.* catalogue entries for the two codes.

findings_addressed.what_changed: ChangeEmailDto now requires `currentPassword`; EmailVerificationService.requestEmailChange verifies it (uniform-time dummyVerify on the no-hash path) before anything is staged. The token payload records `prevEmail` and the apply step pins it in the where-clause — `updateMany({ where: { id, tenantId, email: prevEmail } })` — so a change staged during a stolen session is inert once the owner has recovered; a pre-deploy token without the claim keeps the old unpinned behaviour so in-flight changes don't all break on release day. The apply write stamps `sessionsValidAfter` ATOMICALLY with the address (so a crash can't leave the change applied and sessions alive) and then calls revokeAllForUser to drop AuthGuard's 60s positive cache: the attacker's borrowed cookie dies and the real owner is signed out, which is the visible signal. Because EMAIL_DRIVER is console and nothing is delivered, the notice lands in TWO reachable places: a plain-text security notice enqueued to the OLD address (a durable email_outbox row, readable at the operator's /admin/outbox escape hatch) AND an `account.email_change_requested` row in the LIBRARY's own audit log, which its owner/admin reads at Settings → Activity (GET /t/:slug/audit). A second audit row `account.email_changed` is written when the change lands. Verified end-to-end in the integration spec: outbox row addressed to the previous address and containing the new one, plus the audit row with {from,to}. Nothing depends on mail arriving.
findings_addressed.residual_risk: The finding also asked for TOTP step-up — tenant-side MFA does not exist in the product, so only the password is available. It also asked for a 'revoke link' in the notice; instead the change is inert until confirmed, applying it signs every device out, and the notice tells the reader to change their password. No revoke-token endpoint was added. No web UI calls /auth/change-email today, so nothing shipped is broken by the new required field.

findings_addressed.what_changed: POST /admin/mfa/setup now reads mfaEnabled: first enrollment is unchanged (there is nothing to step up from), but RE-enrollment requires `currentPassword` AND `currentTotp`, verified against the CURRENTLY stored secret via MfaService.verifyTokenOnce so a shoulder-surfed code cannot be replayed into it. The step-up is recorded on the Redis pending entry (`{secret, steppedUp}`), and POST /admin/mfa/verify refuses to persist a replacement whose pending entry is not marked stepped-up — so the gate cannot be skipped by calling verify directly with a pre-planted secret (covered by its own test). A replacement stamps adminUser.sessionsValidAfter (killing every other admin cookie — AdminAuthGuard already read that column and, until now, nothing ever wrote it) and re-mints the enrolling browser's cookie via AdminSessionService/AdminCookieService so the bump doesn't log out the session that just proved more than a cookie is worth. Deliberately NOT stamped on first enrollment: there were no MFA-blessed cookies to kill and it would sign the admin out mid-flow. The 'email the admin' half is satisfied by a control-plane admin audit row (admin.mfa.enrolled / admin.mfa.replaced / admin.mfa.recovery_codes_reissued via recordAdminAudit) rather than undeliverable mail. An unreadable stored secret (rotated/lost MFA_MASTER_KEY) returns 401 pointing at recovery codes instead of a 500. The stale docblock advertising POST /admin/mfa/disable is gone, replaced by a note saying the route does not exist and why.
findings_addressed.residual_risk: The admin MFA UI (apps/web) offers no re-enrollment flow at all today, so the new step-up fields have no form to be typed into — an admin replacing a factor must call the endpoint directly until the UI adds password + current-code inputs.

findings_addressed.what_changed: login() now reads users.lockedUntil and refuses a CORRECT password while it is in the future (silently, same generic 401 as every other path, dummyVerify burned for timing parity) — the column was selected at :102 and never read, so an operator's documented `UPDATE users SET "lockedUntil" = now() + interval '1 hour'` incident response did literally nothing. recordFailure no longer swallows the DB increment error (that counter is the only input the backstop has) and no longer swallows the Redis error: on a Redis failure it calls recordDegradedFailure, which writes lockedUntil = now + LOGIN_LOCKOUT_MS once failedLogins reaches MAX_FAILED_LOGINS, and logs at ERROR. The DB lock engages ONLY on the Redis-failure path, and that confinement is the whole design: a bare-account lock is a renewable DoS anyone can point at a named librarian, which is exactly why A1-01 moved the lock to per-(account+IP) Redis. An attacker cannot choose to be in the degraded branch, and while they are, the alternative is unlimited guessing at every account (RateLimitService.hit also fails open for the login bucket). This makes rate-limit.service.ts:38-42's claim that 'per-account lockout (LoginService) is the backstop' true rather than requiring the comment to be deleted. A successful login still clears lockedUntil.
findings_addressed.residual_risk: During a Redis outage the DB lock IS account-wide, so an attacker guessing at one account can lock that librarian out for LOGIN_LOCKOUT_MS. Deliberate and documented in the code: bounded in time, self-clearing on a correct sign-in once expired, requires an outage to reach, and strictly better than the zero protection that exists today. rate-limit.service.ts is out of my file set so its comment is unchanged (it is now accurate).

findings_addressed.what_changed: Built the code half that was missing: MfaRecoveryService issues ten single-use recovery codes (20 chars of Crockford-ish base32 = 100 bits, grouped for transcription) at MFA enrollment and on demand at POST /admin/mfa/recovery-codes (same step-up as replacing the factor — whoever can mint bypasses can bypass). Only SHA-256 digests are stored, compared with timingSafeEqual; bcrypt would put 2.5s into every recovery login for no benefit against a 100-bit secret. Wired into the REAL entry point: POST /admin/auth/login accepts `recoveryCode` in place of `totp`, consumes it (a code that cannot be burned is REFUSED — a reusable recovery code is a second static password), counts a bad one as a failed attempt so the ADM-5 lockout still applies, and logs the redemption at warn. GET /admin/mfa/status reports recoveryCodesRemaining so 'we have no way back in' is visible before the phone is lost. Storage is a platform_settings row (`admin.mfa.recovery:<adminId>`) because packages/db-control/prisma/schema.prisma is out of my file set; the value is versioned (v:1) so a later move to an AdminUser column is a copy of these rows. No migration added.
findings_addressed.residual_risk: Two halves remain and both are outside my file set. (1) The codes are RETURNED by POST /admin/mfa/verify but no UI displays them — until MfaEnrollForm.tsx renders them once, an operator enrolling through the browser never sees them, and the admin sign-in page has no field to type one into. (2) The finding's own fix is operational: a SECOND owner-tier admin on a separate device, and the recovery procedure written into server-handbook.md Part 10. scripts/bootstrap-admin.ts and the handbook are out of scope. Storing per-admin secrets in platform_settings is a deliberate compromise, not the right long-term home.

verdicts.reasoning: Reproduced the audit probe against the API under NODE_ENV=production: /auth/me 200 → POST /auth/logout 204 → SAME cookie on /auth/me = 401 AND on /t/<slug>/members = 401 (the tenant route returned 200 with a live cookie one line earlier, so the 401 is the revocation and not a broken fixture). POST /auth/sessions/revoke-all exists and is wired (204, both sessions dead, verified in their spec which I ran). Per-session scoping is real (second session survives). With SESSION_TTL_SEC at its 7-day default a token minted milliseconds earlier can never satisfy it. new_problems.issue: The degraded DB lockout keys on `users.failedLogins`, which is a LIFETIME counter — it is only ever reset to 0 by a successful sign-in (line 162), a password reset, or an admin staff reset, and never decays with the Redis window. So an account that has accumulated five or more failed sign-ins over its life (typos across months, a shared circulation-desk username) is locked out for the full LOGIN_LOCKOUT_MS on its very FIRST mistyped password during any Redis blip, not after five. The threshold the code reads as 'five failures in this incident' is 'five failures ever'. This also makes the acknowledged degraded-mode DoS materially cheaper than the code comment describes.
new_problems.reproduction: Set a user's failedLogins to 8 in the control DB (or simply accumulate them: `failedLogins` is never decremented). Make Redis unreachable. The account is now account-wide locked after a single typo. Their own unit spec at login-lockout.spec.ts:117 encodes this shape (failedLogins seeded at 4, one failure → lock).

fix.summary: Eight webhook and plan-change defects addressed in apps/api/src/billing/**, apps/web/.../billing/PlanGrid.tsx and docs/billing-go-live.md. Five are fully fixed (billing-05, -06, -07, -09, -12); three are partial because their remaining half lives in a file this package does not own (billing-10's PATCH validator in admin-plans.controller.ts, billing-11's CHECK-constraint migration in packages/db-control, billing-14's admin SubscriptionsToggle.tsx). One half of billing-05 and most of billing-14's stated impact were already closed by earlier rounds — evidence below, not a claim. 39 new tests, every bug-detecting one mutation-verified to fail against the pre-fix behaviour. No migration, no schema change, no new translation key (el/en parity check passes). The API was re-booted under all three shipped postures (STRIPE_DRIVER=none, legacy fake-on-production, real) and starts in each; the new admin route is mapped and owner-gated.

findings_addressed.what_changed: HALF WAS ALREADY FIXED: `git show HEAD:apps/api/src/billing/billing.service.ts` line 1000 already keyed the webhook's graceUntil on Stripe's raw `payload.status === 'past_due'`, so an `incomplete` subscription got past_due with graceUntil null and the resolver (effective-plan.service.ts:255 requires `past_due AND graceUntil > NOW()`) granted nothing. My diff does not touch that block; a regression test now locks it. THE LIVE HALF was the invoice path: `invoice.payment_failed` -> recordPaymentFailure armed `now + 7d` unconditionally, so the first invoice of a never-paid subscription still bought 7 days of the paid tier. recordPaymentFailure now takes a REQUIRED `evidence: { hasSettledInvoice }` (no default), derived by handleStripeInvoiceFailed from the invoice's `billing_reason`: only `subscription_cycle`/`subscription_update`/`subscription_threshold` count as proof somebody paid. Unknown or absent reason resolves to FALSE (unproven), and an already-running window from a genuine renewal failure is preserved rather than torn down.
findings_addressed.residual_risk: `billing_reason` is the evidence, not a settled-invoice ledger. A renewal failure on a subscription whose only prior invoice was voided would still be treated as proven. A durable per-subscription "has ever settled" column would be exact and needs a packages/db-control migration.

findings_addressed.what_changed: The stale-replay guard now orders by the ENVELOPE, not the period. `StripeWebhookEvent` gained `created`; `stripeEventContext(event)` lifts it; StripeWebhookController.dispatch passes it to syncStripeSubscription (asserted in stripe-webhook.controller.spec.ts, and the sampleEvent fixture now carries `created` so a missing wire cannot pass). billing.service keeps the newest applied `event.created` per subscription id in Redis (`billing:subevent:<id>`, 90d) and refuses a strictly-older event. The pre-existing period-start comparison stays as the durable first line. For the RETRY-SWEEP path, which re-dispatches a stored `data.object` with no envelope, the service asks Stripe (`getSubscription`) whenever the event would MOVE the plan of a subscription we already track, and refuses the event if Stripe is already on a different price — fail-soft, so an unreachable Stripe leaves pre-fix behaviour rather than erroring a webhook. No Stripe call is spent on a replay that would not move the plan.
findings_addressed.residual_risk: apps/api/src/jobs/stripe-retry.job.ts is outside this package, so the sweep still calls `syncStripeSubscription(obj)` without the envelope — it has `event.created` in hand (`row.payloadJson`) and just does not pass it. The Stripe-authority fallback covers the sweep in production (the sweep returns early under the `disabled` posture and dev/test uses the fake, so the sweep only ever runs with RealStripeDriver), but it is a network round trip rather than a timestamp compare. One-line change named in out_of_scope_files_needed. Redis loss degrades the guard to the pre-existing period comparison, never to something worse.

findings_addressed.what_changed: New private `tenantForStripeCustomer(customer, context)` refuses any payload whose `customer` is not a non-empty string, logs at error level naming the context, and returns null BEFORE Prisma is touched — so `findFirst({ stripeCustomerId: null })` can never render as `stripeCustomerId IS NULL` and match one of the 44 tenants signup leaves with a null customer id. Wired into all four entry points: syncStripeSubscription, handleStripeSubscriptionDeleted, tenantForSubscriptionInvoice (both invoice handlers) and handleCheckoutSessionCompleted. Checkout now also prefers a validated non-empty `client_reference_id` over the customer lookup, per the finding's own recommendation.
findings_addressed.residual_risk: None known. The guard is on every path that reads `payload.customer`; a grep for `stripeCustomerId: payload.customer` in apps/api/src/billing returns nothing.

findings_addressed.what_changed: Three changes. (1) `StripeCustomerInput.idempotencyKey` is a REQUIRED field (not optional, not defaulted) and RealStripeDriver passes it as the Stripe `Idempotency-Key`; ensureStripeCustomer sends `libriant:customer:<tenantId>`, so two concurrent starts receive the SAME customer and the duplicate is never created. (2) The local write is now a conditional `updateMany({ where: { tenantId, stripeCustomerId: null } })`; a racer whose claim matches nothing re-reads and ADOPTS the winner's id (returning it, so Checkout opens on the customer the row holds), logging at error level if the two ids differ. The `create` branch survives only for a tenant with no billing_accounts row. (3) `checkout.session.completed` reconciles `client_reference_id` -> `customer`: it fills a NULL customer id from the session that just completed and never overwrites one we already track, reporting a genuine mismatch at error level instead.
findings_addressed.residual_risk: Stripe idempotency keys are scoped to 24h; two creates more than a day apart could still diverge, which is why the adopt-the-winner path and the checkout reconcile both exist. A unique-index rejection on the reconcile write is caught and logged rather than failing the webhook, because the subscription pointer in the same handler must still land.

findings_addressed.what_changed: (1) `hasStripePrice`/`hasStripeAnnualPrice` no longer mean `!!id`: new exported `isUsableStripePriceId` requires a `price_` prefix and rejects `price_seed_*`, so the vacuous signal is gone from listAvailablePlans. (2) `startCheckout` refuses a placeholder price id server-side with a message naming the fix, so hiding the button is not the only guard. (3) NEW reconciliation that can actually fail: `BillingService.auditPriceCatalogue()` behind `GET /admin/billing/price-catalogue` (BillingCatalogController, AdminAuthGuard + AdminRolesGuard + @AdminRoles('owner')), registered in billing.module.ts and confirmed mapped at boot. It asks Stripe (new `StripeDriver.getPrice`, implemented on all three drivers) about every id and reports plain-language problems for: missing Price, archived Price, currency mismatch, integer minor-unit amount mismatch, interval/interval_count not matching the column it sits in, and the same id in both columns (which Postgres accepts — both unique indexes are satisfied). A free/manual plan is reported as a NOTE, not a problem, so `.ok` can reach true. (4) docs/billing-go-live.md records that the old `hasStripeAnnualPrice: true` step could not fail and points at the new endpoint.
findings_addressed.residual_risk: `PATCH /admin/plans/:slug` still accepts any string into either price column — the audit catches a bad id after the fact, nothing refuses it at write time. That validator belongs in apps/api/src/admin/admin-plans.controller.ts, which this package does not own.

findings_addressed.what_changed: PlanGrid.tsx gained the free-plan branch it lacked, placed ABOVE the `!hasStripePrice` test (isCurrent -> isManual -> isFree -> !hasStripePrice -> upgrade), posting to `/billing/select` and calling `router.refresh()`. It reuses the existing `billing.actions.switchTo` key, so no catalog change and no translation drift. Server side, `selectPlan` now treats a free choice by a PAYING library as a cancellation: it stamps planSelectedAt and delegates to `cancelAtPeriodEnd`, so Stripe stops the renewal and the library keeps the features it has paid for until the period ends, with `customer.subscription.deleted` moving the row. `startCheckout` refuses any plan with `monthlyPriceCents <= 0` outright. fix.summary:
All four findings fixed and proven by execution. The two "no unique constraint" findings (data-integrity-03, -06) are closed by one guarded, idempotent tenant migration that de-duplicates deliberately where it is provably safe and REFUSES atomically where it is not, plus P2002 recovery in the importer so the new constraints turn lost races into skips rather than failed rows. data-integrity-05 is closed in two halves: the engine now claims a copy under the shared `book:<id>` advisory lock and writes a real pickup deadline (or demotes the hold to `queued` with a warning), and a second migration repairs the immortal holds already sitting in customer databases. input-and-files-06 is closed with a per-tenant staging budget refused before a byte is written, plus the first sweeper that has ever deleted anything from STORAGE_ROOT/_imports, wired into the queue service's existing periodic timer.

One defect in my own first draft is worth naming because it is exactly the failure mode this remediation was warned about: the P2002 matcher was written against the INDEX name, which Prisma never reports (`meta.target` is undefined; only the message names the COLUMN). It compiled, read correctly, and did nothing. The four-way concurrent-import test caught it. A second self-inflicted bug — catching P2002 inside a Prisma `$transaction` and re-reading on the aborted tx — was caught by reasoning about Postgres 25P02 before it shipped, and the recovery was moved outside the transaction as a single retry.

Also fixed en route: both migrations originally used bare `now()`, which on this Europe/Athens server writes LOCAL wall time into `timestamp(3) WITHOUT time zone` columns that Prisma fills with UTC. Measured: the first apply stamped an audit_log row 00:18 against a Node clock of 21:41. Every timestamp is now `now() AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'`.

BLOCKING PREREQUISITE: apps/api/src/catalog/authors.service.ts (out of my ownership) has zero P2002 handling, so once `authors_sortname_unique_active` deploys, a librarian typing an existing author's name gets a 500 instead of a 409. That must land before the migration deploys.

findings_addressed.what_changed: New migration `20260826090000_catalog_natural_key_uniqueness` creates `books_isbn13_unique_active` — a partial unique index on `books(isbn13) WHERE isbn13 IS NOT NULL AND "archivedAt" IS NULL`, matching the scope of the existing `book_copies_barcode_unique_active`. Live data is handled in three ordered stages before any DDL: STAGE 0 detects duplicate-ISBN groups in which MORE THAN ONE active record already carries copies or holds and RAISEs with the offending ISBNs, a runnable diagnostic query and the resolution — folding those together would re-point physical items and live queue positions, which is a circulation change, not a schema change. Because prisma wraps the file in a transaction the refusal rolls back everything, so there is no half-applied state. STAGE 2 then archives the provably-bare duplicates (survivor = the record holding the copies/holds if one does, else the oldest), writing a `book.deduplicated` audit_log row naming the survivor. Nothing is deleted; the archive is reversible and is exactly the repair the audit describes doing by hand. In the engine, `commitBook` now catches a P2002 on the ISBN key, returns the optimistically-claimed quota slot, re-reads the winner and routes into the shared `resolveBookDuplicate` (skip/update/error) instead of failing the row; `findBookByIsbn` and `resolveBook` gained `orderBy [createdAt, id]` so a database still carrying pre-migration duplicates resolves them consistently instead of by coin flip.
findings_addressed.residual_risk: STAGE 0 can refuse a tenant whose catalogue has two ISBN-sharing records that BOTH carry copies, wedging that tenant's migration history until an operator resolves it. That is the deliberate choice over silently merging circulation data; the exception message carries the ISBNs, a runnable listing query and the fix, and I verified the recovery path (resolve, re-run, succeeds). Also: `BooksService.create` now returns a generic 409 "That conflicts with an existing record." on a duplicate ISBN rather than naming the ISBN — correct status, vague message. Reported as an owner action.

findings_addressed.what_changed: Same migration creates `authors_sortname_unique_active` on `authors("sortName") WHERE "archivedAt" IS NULL`. STAGE 1 folds existing duplicates deterministically and losslessly: survivor = oldest non-archived row for the sortName (tie-broken by id), `book_authors` links that would collide on the (bookId, authorId) primary key after the move are dropped, every remaining link is re-pointed to the survivor, an `author.deduplicated` audit_log row is written per loser, and the losers are archived rather than deleted. Authors have no unsafe case — a book_authors row is a pure join row — so STAGE 1 always succeeds. In the engine, `commitAuthor` recovers from a lost create race via the new shared `resolveAuthorDuplicate`, and `findAuthorId` orders deterministically. Critically, `writeBook` now retries its transaction ONCE on an author-key P2002: the violation aborts the whole Postgres transaction (25P02 on every later statement), so recovery cannot happen inside it — the naive in-transaction re-read I wrote first would have thrown, losing an entirely valid book row whenever a librarian added an author while an import mentioned them.
findings_addressed.residual_risk: apps/api/src/catalog/authors.service.ts has NO P2002 handling at all (`create` and `update` are bare `client.author.*`), so after this migration deploys a duplicate author name typed in the UI becomes a 500 with a supportCode rather than a 409. That file is outside this package's ownership; it is a REQUIRED owner action before deploy and is written into the migration header.

findings_addressed.what_changed: Two halves. (1) The engine: `commitReservation` now routes `status='ready'` into a new `commitReadyHold`, which takes the same `book:<bookId>` advisory lock every live allocation path uses (A7-01), CAS-claims an `available` copy (flipping it to `reserved`, exactly as `promoteNextHoldInTx` does), sets `fulfilledByCopyId`, and gives the hold a real `expiresAt` — the file's date when it is usable, otherwise `readyAt + tenant_settings.holdPickupHours`, which is also read in `init()`. A file date that violates the `reservations_expires_after_ready` CHECK is defaulted with a warning instead of failing the row. When no copy is free the hold is written as `queued` at the back of the line with a `downgraded_to_queued` warning, because "ready" would be a lie; the validate pass predicts the same demotion (tracking copies notionally claimed by earlier rows in the file) so the librarian learns before the commit, not after. `findPriorReservation` now treats `queued` and `ready` as ONE slot when the file carries no placed date — without that, a re-import of a demoted row would miss its own write and then trip `reservations_one_active_per_book_member`, turning a clean skip into a mystifying row error. (2) New migration `20260826085000_repair_orphan_ready_holds` fixes the rows the OLD importer already wrote into customer databases, which no code change can reach: per book, under the same advisory lock, each orphan ready hold either claims a free copy and gets a real deadline, or is demoted to `queued` at the back of the queue behind existing legitimate holds — oldest offer first, `reservation.repaired` audit row each. It is ordered BEFORE the catalogue migration on purpose, so a wedged patron does not wait on an unrelated catalogue merge that might refuse.
findings_addressed.residual_risk: A demoted hold still blocks renewals of that title, which is correct behaviour for a genuine queued hold but is a behaviour change from the (broken) ready state. Repaired holds that had to be queued are only offered a copy when the ordinary promote-on-return path next runs; the migration does not force-promote beyond the copies actually free at migration time.

findings_addressed.what_changed: Two lines of defence, both wired. (a) `ImportService.createBatch` calls a new `assertStagingBudget` as its FIRST action — before the preview parse and before a byte reaches disk — refusing with a 409 when the tenant already holds IMPORT_MAX_STAGED_BATCHES (3) staged uploads or when the incoming file would push their staged total over IMPORT_MAX_STAGED_BYTES (128 MB). The count stops a retry storm of small files; the byte budget stops a couple of huge ones. (b) `ImportQueueService.sweepAbandonedStaging` runs on the service's existing periodic timer (both sweeps now go through a new `runSweeps`, each isolated so one failing does not stop the other). It has two passes: by row, deleting the file and blanking `stagingPath` for batches idle past IMPORT_STAGING_TTL_MS (24 h) — the batch row and its issue report survive, only the bytes go; and by directory, using a new `listStagedFiles()` to delete files older than the TTL that NO batch row claims, which is the only way to reach the crash window between `stageFile` writing bytes and the row recording the path. To make the budget's arithmetic truthful, every path that deletes a staged file now blanks `stagingPath` in the same write (worker finish, cancel-mid-run in BOTH phases), and `requireRunnable` refuses a swept batch with "upload it again" instead of letting the worker die on ENOENT. I also closed a bypass the finding did not name: `cancel()` on an `uploaded` batch moved the row out of every counted state while its 64 MB stayed on disk forever — it now deletes the file, except when a job may be mid-read, where the worker's own cancel path does it.
findings_addressed.residual_risk: The budget is per tenant, not global: N tenants can still each hold their 128 MB, so this bounds the blast radius rather than guaranteeing the volume never fills. No free-disk check exists anywhere in apps/api/src (the audit noted this too); a global watermark would be the next step and is out of scope here.

fix.summary:
Five medium performance findings worked against a purpose-built Institutional-sized scratch tenant (400k books / 520k copies / 100k members / 2M loans / 40k holds, 1,393 MB — matching the audit's own seed) on the audit Postgres at :55440. Every plan below is EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) of the literal statement Prisma emits, captured from Prisma's query event log, before and after.

FIXED OUTRIGHT: performance-08 (the hourly overdue sweeps) and performance-12 (the sub-trigram search term, for the catalogue).
PARTIAL, with the remainder named and patched-in-words: performance-05 (the interceptor pays the same count on the route, and the index is a tenant migration), performance-07 (only one of the six tables has a written-down period), performance-11 (the API half is built, mounted and tested; the web page still calls the five list endpoints).

Three things the findings got wrong, all measured:
1. performance-11's suggested fix is a REGRESSION. `count(*) FILTER (WHERE …) FROM loans` is a Parallel Seq Scan — 32,587 buffers, 90.983 ms — because FILTER is per-row and leaves the aggregate with no WHERE to seek on. Written as five separate subqueries each predicate stays indexable: 17,102 buffers, 62 ms. The shipped endpoint uses the latter.
2. performance-08's "scans the whole loans table" half is ALREADY FIXED by performance-02's `loans_status_dueAt_id_idx`. The predicate is now a Bitmap Index Scan, 386 buffers, 2.8 ms — not the 32,845-buffer seq scan quoted. What was left was the buffering and the N+1, which is what I fixed.
3. The obvious way to page that sweep is also a regression. Prisma's expressible keyset (`dueAt > x OR (dueAt = x AND id > y)`) is not a btree start key: at page 30 it was `Rows Removed by Filter: 14500, Buffers: shared hit=9094`, worse than the unbounded query. Both paged sweeps therefore use a raw row-value predicate `("dueAt","id") > ($1,$2)`, which seeks (239 buffers, flat with depth).

Verification: apps/api unit 728/728 green (78 files); apps/api integration 171/171 green (25 files) including 21 in performance-hot-paths.spec.ts. Every new acceptance test was mutation-checked — five deliberate reversions of the fixed code (skip-when-unlimited, the short-term early return, the keyset page advance, the dedup pre-filter, the processed-only prune) each made the corresponding test fail, and all were restored. The control-plane migration was applied three times against a scratch database (second and third runs are no-ops) and survives a pg_dump -Fc / pg_restore round trip with the partial index intact. `pnpm check:translations` passes.

findings_addressed.what_changed: BooksService now resolves `max_books` through EffectivePlanService BEFORE opening the create/un-archive transaction, and when the limit is the UNLIMITED_INT sentinel it skips both the `pg_advisory_xact_lock('quota:<tenant>:max_books:')` and the `count(*) FROM books WHERE "archivedAt" IS NULL` entirely — there is no ceiling to race for, so there is nothing to serialise and nothing to count. That is the SHIPPED posture (BILLING_ENABLED=false makes every int feature unlimited), so today it removes the whole cost. When the limit is finite the existing race-safe path is byte-for-byte unchanged. Measured baseline, on the literal statement Prisma emits for `book.count` (`SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT id FROM books WHERE "archivedAt" IS NULL OFFSET 0) sub`), 400,000-title tenant: `Aggregate … Seq Scan on books, Buffers: shared hit=1594 read=11739, Execution Time: 59.142 ms` — 13,333 buffers, 104 MB, through a 128 MB shared_buffers pool every library on the box shares. I also tested and REJECTED the obvious cheaper count: `SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT 1 FROM books WHERE "archivedAt" IS NULL LIMIT $cap)` looks 80x cheaper in isolation but only because the seed is over the cap — whenever the create is ALLOWED the library is under its ceiling, the LIMIT is never reached, and the scan runs to completion exactly as before. It is not a fix.
findings_addressed.residual_risk: TWO pieces remain, both outside this change's file ownership and both reported below. (1) QuotaInterceptor (apps/api/src/plans/quota.interceptor.ts) runs QUOTA_COUNTERS.max_books — the SAME 13,333-buffer full scan — unconditionally on every POST /catalog/books, before the service is entered. So at the HTTP level a book create still pays one scan even under an unlimited ceiling. One-line fix given in owner_actions. (2) With billing ON and a finite ceiling the in-transaction count is still a full scan until the tenant carries a partial index; I measured the candidate: `CREATE INDEX books_active_idx ON books (id) WHERE "archivedAt" IS NULL` turns it into `Index Only Scan using books_active_idx, Heap Fetches: 0, Buffers: shared hit=1 read=1527, Execution Time: 30.306 ms` — 1,528 buffers instead of 13,333, an 8.7x reduction. packages/db-tenant/prisma/** is owned by another change (two agents are writing tenant migrations concurrently), so the DDL is handed over rather than applied.

findings_addressed.what_changed: Added the ONE limb the instruction permits — a period that is actually written down. Three places in the tree assert a 30-day prune of `stripe_webhook_events` and none of them did it: packages/db-control/prisma/schema.prisma on `payloadJson` ("Raw event body for replay / debug. Pruned after 30 days."), and apps/api/src/jobs/stripe-retry.job.ts twice ("Rows are bounded: the table is cleaned at 30 days", and "a table that is pruned at 30 days" — which is that job's stated justification for running an unindexed COUNT over it every five minutes). `sweepRetention` now clears the body of processed events past 30 days, in bounded batches, and the run message and `counts.stripePayloadsPruned` report it. Two deliberate narrowings, both in the code comment: the ROW is kept forever because `persistEvent` in stripe-webhook.controller.ts reads `processedAt` off it as the durable replay guard that survives a Redis outage — deleting it would re-arm a re-dispatch of a >30-day-old "Resend" from the Stripe Dashboard, writing a stale subscription payload over a current one; and rows that never processed keep their body, because those are the `abandoned` backlog and the payload is the only thing an operator can replay from. Migration 20260826113000_stripe_webhook_payload_retention adds the work-queue index. Measured on a 50,000-row / 100 MB replica of the real DDL (2 KB payloads, three years of events, 2% unprocessed), on the statement the job issues, AFTER a full prune pass — i.e. the state every run but the first meets: without the index `Seq Scan … Buffers: shared hit=9401 read=3501, Execution Time: 15.476 ms`; with it `Bitmap Index Scan on stripe_webhook_events_prunable_idx, Buffers: shared read=2, Execution Time: 0.020 ms`. 12,902 buffers versus 2, daily, against the control database every library shares. The predicate carries all three conditions including `payloadJson <> '{}'`, so a pruned row leaves the index and the queue empties itself.
findings_addressed.residual_risk: The other five tables named by the finding — control-plane `audit_log`, `email_outbox`, `announcement_deliveries`, `stripe_webhook_events` ROWS, `support_redemption_attempts` (and `support_sessions`) — still have no sweep, and deliberately so: I searched the whole tree and every period that would govern them is an unfilled `[PLACEHOLDER]` in locales/{el,en}/legal/privacy.md §6 (`[30]` days, `[14]`-day backups, `[up to 5–10]` years, `[a limited period, e.g. 90 days]`). fix.summary:
All five findings addressed. Three fixed outright (07, 08, 11); two partial (09, 10) where the residual is either an apps/web UI feature or a commercial figure I must not invent.

privacy-legal-07 — the export path now carries the same consent-and-audit model as support impersonation, and I decided AGAINST making it weaker. A scope='tenant' export requires an active, tenant-issued SupportKey session for that library (refused 403 otherwise); every admin export writes a mandatory control-plane AuditEvent AND a mandatory row in the library's own audit_log (viaSupport-flagged), enqueues a disclosure e-mail, and is refused if the record cannot be written — disclose-then-enqueue, with the job row deleted again on failure. scope='all' cannot be consented to by any one library, so instead it fans out a row into EVERY included library's audit_log and the control row names the ones that could not be told. Downloads are audit-logged before a byte streams. publicExportJob now exposes requestedByKind, so the library's own export list attributes a Libriant-initiated export instead of showing it unattributed. Reasoning for the "why not weaker" question, and why this does not contradict the impersonation `export-write` deny rule, is written into export-consent.ts.

privacy-legal-11 — support impersonation is now described where a library would look: DPA Annex I (§2 nature/purpose), Annex II (§6.2 mechanics: who issues the key, 60-minute key, 4-hour session, MFA, what we may not do inside it, what is logged on both sides, where the log lives, retention), §6.3 (administrative exports), §6.4 (paste-ready wording for the library's own member notice), and Privacy §10. Both locales, Greek first.

privacy-legal-08 — docs/legal/ropa.{el,en}.md written from what the system actually does. Section 7 deliberately splits retention into "enforced today, by this named job" (applications 12mo, tenant audit_log per plan, exports 24h/2h, temps 30min, backups 14d, sessions 4h/keys 60min) and "not determined — needs counsel" (5 marked placeholders), and states the trap that with subscriptions OFF the audit_log retention resolves to unlimited so the sweep deletes nothing. Art. 30(5) exemption analysed and rejected on all three limbs.

privacy-legal-09 — acceptance is now evidenced, not just recorded. Every published version has a frozen, version-addressed copy of all seven documents in both locales under docs/legal/accepted/<LEGAL_VERSION>/, their SHA-256 compiled into the API, and signup writes a tenant.legal_accepted audit row (locale, who accepted, per-document digest + archive path) INSIDE the tenant-creation transaction — a library cannot exist without the evidence of what it agreed to.

privacy-legal-10 — the structural defect is fixed: the cap is now "the greater of (a) 12 months' fees and (b) [EUR MINIMUM LIABILITY CAP]", explicitly a floor and not a fallback, so it can never resolve to zero during the twelve-months-free launch; §10.1 carries an express Art. 82 carve-out. Terms §2.4 adds the public-body acceptance clause and the counter-signed-instrument path.

Everything green: 728 API unit tests, my 9 integration tests, tsc clean in api/web/shared, eslint and prettier clean on changed files, check:legal and check:translations pass.

For scope='all' it fans a row into every non-archived tenant's audit_log (best-effort per tenant, since one unreachable tenant DB must not veto a platform operation) and records tenantsNotified/tenantsNotFound in the control row so a partial notification cannot be silent. notifyLibraryOfExport() enqueues a disclosure e-mail to the tenant's primaryEmail (best-effort, kind 'transactional' so no enum migration; nothing depends on it arriving). ExportService.createForAdmin's first parameter changed from a bare adminId string to a REQUIRED ExportRequester {adminId, ip, userAgent} — a forgettable optional argument is how the ip/ua would have silently stayed null. Order is gate → create job → disclose → e-mail → enqueue, and a disclosure failure deletes the job row and rethrows, so no export can run whose record failed to write. Art. 30(2)'s required contents are all present: controller categories (§2, the six library_type values), categories of processing (§3, fourteen rows each an operation the product performs), categories of data subject and data (§4), recipients and sub-processors with locations and safeguards (§6: Hetzner / Cloudflare / Stripe / e-mail), third-country transfers (§6), retention (§7), and a general description of the Art. 32(1) measures (§8). Art. 30(1) controller-side processing is separated into §9. The Art. 30(5) exemption is analysed and rejected on all three limbs, correctly.

Every provider identity value is a marked [PLACEHOLDER] — none invented, as instructed — and §5 states plainly that nothing in the product branches on age, which is the uncomfortable fact a template would have omitted.
verdicts.bypass: The record's own placeholders live under docs/ and `pnpm check:legal` scans only locales/*/legal/, so the ROPA's ~11 unfilled values are tracked by a hand-maintained list in §0 rather than by the script. check:legal still exits 0. Reported under new_problems as a drift risk, not a failure of this finding.

verdicts.reasoning:
The half that was ASKED FOR here is genuinely and rigorously fixed, and I proved it independently — but the INDEX finding is a conjunction and two of its limbs are untouched in production code, so I will not call the finding closed. The implementer's own status is 'partial' and I agree with it.

What IS fixed, verified three ways. (1) I reimplemented apps/web/lib/legal.ts's stripAuthorNote() from scratch and hashed the live locales markdown against the committed docs/legal/accepted/2026-08-26/ archive: all 14 files byte-identical, all 14 digests present in LEGAL_CORPUS. The freeze is real and is the published body, not the raw file. (2) I ran the integration spec: two real POST /auth/signup requests (Greek and English) produce a tenant.legal_accepted control-plane audit row whose per-document sha256 values match a freshly computed hash of the live markdown, with the el and en terms digests differing — so the record does distinguish which text was shown. (3) The row is created inside the same controlDb.$transaction as the Tenant and owner User (signup.service.ts:186), so a library cannot exist without it. LEGAL_VERSION was correctly bumped, and legal-acceptance.spec.ts triangulates three separate files on disk so a future silent one-word edit fails the suite.

What is NOT fixed, and it is the pattern the brief warns about. `grep -rn readLegalAcceptance apps/api/src apps/web` returns exactly ONE hit: the definition. It has no HTTP route and no caller outside the test. `grep -rn legalAcceptedVersion` still returns only the two writes in signup.service.ts and the schema declarations — no reader, no login-time comparison against LEGAL_VERSION, no re-acceptance prompt, no admin screen. The finding's title is 'recorded but not evidenced: one global version string, written once, NEVER READ, with no archived copy and NO RE-ACCEPTANCE FLOW'; the archived-copy limb is closed, the never-read and no-re-acceptance limbs are exactly as they were, and LEGAL_VERSION is still one stamp over all seven documents rather than the per-document version the fix text asked for. This is machinery built and not mounted — disclosed honestly in the docblock and the report rather than hidden, which is the difference from the precedents, but the finding does not close on it.
verdicts.bypass: Any library that already accepted 2026-06-22 is now stamped against a version nothing prompts them to re-accept — nothing in the code detects the mismatch because nothing reads the column. Harmless only because there is no production data. Separately, the DTO's defaultLocale is optional and acceptanceLocale() falls back to 'el', so a direct API signup that omits it records the Greek corpus regardless of what was shown; the web form always sends the browsing locale and links /${locale}/legal/*, so the shipped path is correct.

verdicts.reasoning:
The structural defect the verification upheld is repaired in both locales, and repaired in the way that survives the placeholder still being empty — which is the right call given the instruction not to invent a commercial figure.

§10.3 went from 'capped at the fees you paid or owed in the 12 months … (or [EUR amount] where no fees were paid)' to 'capped at the **greater of** (a) the fees … and (b) [EUR MINIMUM LIABILITY CAP]', followed by an express sentence that limb (b) is 'a **floor, not a fallback**: it applies whenever it is the larger figure, including during any free trial or promotional period'. That is the actual fix: under the old drafting the twelve-months-free launch offer made limb (a) zero and limb (b) inapplicable, so the cap resolved to zero; under the new drafting it cannot, whatever number lands in (b). Greek carries the identical construction (el/terms.md:165-168).

§10.1 gained the Art. 82 carve-out the verification specifically asked for, and it is not a hand-wave — it names death/personal injury, fraud, wilful misconduct and gross negligence, then says a data subject's Art. 82 claim 'is **not** capped, reduced, or apportioned by Sections 10.2 or 10.3, or by anything else in these Terms or the DPA' (el/terms.md:150-158 matches).

On the authority limb, which the verification called a contested opinion rather than a defect: the intro warranty now also requires that any internal step the organisation's rules demand has been completed, and new §2.4 (en:43-50 / el:47) gives public bodies a counter-signed path — 'we will provide these Terms and the DPA as a document for signature by your legal representative, and that signed instrument governs in place of acceptance through the website. We may require it before processing begins.' That is more than was strictly owed and it costs nothing.

[EUR MINIMUM LIABILITY CAP] is correctly left as a marked placeholder and IS reported by check:legal in 2 documents, which is what the brief asked for.
verdicts.bypass: The counter-signed instrument is described in the Terms but nothing records it: there is no tenant-side column or document template for a signed order form, so §2.4's promise is process only. Separately, §12's new frozen-version sentence overstates by one version — see new_problems.

new_problems.issue: The DPA now states as fact something the shipped UI does not do. locales/en/legal/dpa.md:145-146 (and el/dpa.md:172) promises that a Libriant-initiated export "also appears in your own export list at Settings → Export, marked as requested by Libriant rather than by your staff." `publicExportJob` was extended to return `requestedByKind`, but the page that renders that list never consumes it: `ExportJobView` (line 12-23) does not declare the field, the table renders only Format / Status / Size / Created / Download, and there is no `settings.export.cols.requestedBy` key in locales/en/settings.json or locales/el/settings.json. The half-mounted fix is exactly what the audit verification called "a detection channel that cannot tell you WHO", and the integration test does not catch it because it asserts the API JSON (`mine!.requestedByKind === 'admin'`) rather than the page. The library's own audit log DOES carry the disclosure correctly, so the finding is still fixed — but this specific sentence in a binding contract is untrue as shipped.
new_problems.reproduction: Open apps/web/app/[locale]/t/[slug]/settings/export/ExportManager.tsx: `ExportJobView` has no `requestedByKind`, and the <thead> at ~line 136 lists five columns, none of them a requester. `grep -rn requestedByKind apps/web` returns nothing. Then read locales/en/legal/dpa.md:145-146. A librarian following the DPA to Settings → Export sees a row identical to one their own staff started.

new_problems.issue: Terms §12's new sentence overstates the scheme by one version: "Every published version of these Terms and of the documents they incorporate is kept frozen." `ls docs/legal/accepted/` contains only `2026-08-26`. Version 2026-06-22 was a published version (committed at 22e1efa, and the value LEGAL_VERSION carried until this change) and has no frozen directory — it is recoverable only from git history, which is not the version-addressed archive the clause describes. The same sentence appears in the Greek terms. No production tenant accepted 2026-06-22, so the practical impact today is nil, but the clause is a representation about a records system and it is currently false for one prior version.
new_problems.reproduction: `ls docs/legal/accepted/` → `2026-08-26` only. `git log --oneline -1 -- locales/en/legal/terms.md` → 22e1efa, the commit that published the 2026-06-22 text. Compare with locales/en/legal/terms.md:174-178.

new_problems.issue: The ROPA's own unfilled values are tracked by a hand-maintained table in §0 rather than by the tool the brief names as the source of truth. `scripts/check-legal-docs.mjs` scans only `locales/*/legal/`, so the ~11 placeholders in the record ([COMPANY LEGAL NAME], [REGISTERED ADDRESS], [VAT NUMBER], [NAME(S)], the four sub-processor entities, [Region], and the five [RETENTION PERIOD — …] values in §7.2) do not appear in `pnpm check:legal`'s 29-item list. §0 says so honestly, but a hand-maintained list of placeholders is the thing that drifts first: fill one and forget the table, and the record silently claims to be more complete than it is. The implementer lists extending the script as an out-of-scope follow-up.
new_problems.reproduction: `node scripts/check-legal-docs.mjs` → exit 0, "29 unfilled value(s) across 14 document(s)", and no ropa.* file among them. `grep -c '\[' docs/legal/ropa.en.md` shows placeholders the script never sees. Confirm the scan root in scripts/check-legal-docs.mjs.

new_problems.issue: If `discloseAdminExport` throws, the compensating `controlDb.exportJob.delete(...).catch(() => undefined)` swallows its own failure, so a control-DB hiccup on the delete leaves an orphaned `status:'queued'` export_jobs row that is never enqueued and never progresses. For scope='tenant' that row is selected by `listForTenant` (targetTenantId + scope='tenant', no requester filter), so the library's Settings → Export page shows a permanently "queued" export that no one started and that will never complete — an unexplained artifact in the exact surface this finding is about. The window is narrow (the tenant-side audit write failed but the control DB is still writable) but it is the failure mode the disclose-then-enqueue ordering creates.
new_problems.reproduction: Read export.service.ts:137-150. Make `recordTenantSideExport` fail (tenant DB unreachable or read_only) while the control DB is healthy, and make the subsequent delete fail too: the 403/500 goes out, no job is enqueued, and the row created at line 118 survives with status 'queued' and is visible at GET /t/:slug/exports.

new_problems.issue: A `scope:'all'` export does O(tenants) blocking work inside the HTTP request before the job is even enqueued: `fanOutPlatformExport` loops every non-archived tenant sequentially, calling `tenantPrisma.getClient()` (which builds and pools a new PrismaClient on a cache miss, evicting others from a 50-entry LRU) and awaiting one INSERT per tenant, and then `notifyLibraryOfExport` loops them all again with a control-DB read plus an outbox INSERT each. At a few dozen libraries this is seconds; at a few hundred the POST /admin/exports request will time out at the edge before returning 202 — and because the disclosure is (correctly) mandatory, a timeout there means the platform-wide export cannot be started at all. Also, both loops read the tenant list at disclosure time while export-processors.ts re-reads it at worker time, so a library created in between is dumped without a notification.
new_problems.reproduction: Read export-consent.ts:178-201 and 284-337, then export.service.ts:137-158 — all of it is awaited before `this.queue.enqueue(job.id)`. Seed N tenants and time `POST /admin/exports {scope:'all'}`; cost grows linearly with N, with LRU eviction churn (each eviction disconnects a PrismaClient) once N exceeds the cache size.

new_problems.issue: The stated justification for compiling LEGAL_CORPUS into the API image is true today but the deployment is explicitly designed to break it. The docblock argues the web app "serves the documents from the copy baked into its image at build time", and that holds only because the `web` service in infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:281-309 does not set LOCALES_ROOT (so apps/web/lib/legal.ts falls back to the baked /app/locales) — even though that same service DOES bind-mount `../../locales:/srv/libriant/locales:ro`, and apps/web/Dockerfile:52-56 states the intent outright: "the *runtime* stage gets them again via the bind-mount in compose so designers can hot-swap." The moment anyone realises the mount is inert and adds `LOCALES_ROOT: /srv/libriant/locales` to the web service, the served legal text comes from the host checkout while the recorded digests stay pinned to the API image build — and nothing detects the divergence at runtime, because the only thing enforcing agreement is a CI-time unit test against the repo.
new_problems.reproduction: Compare infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:55 (LOCALES_ROOT set in x-app-env, consumed by api and worker) with :290-308 (web's own environment block, no LOCALES_ROOT, yet mounting ../../locales at /srv/libriant/locales), and apps/web/lib/legal.ts:19-21. Add LOCALES_ROOT to the web service and edit a file in the host checkout without rebuilding the API image: /legal/terms serves the new text, the acceptance row records the old digest, no test or runtime check fires.

fix.summary: Eight of nine findings changed code; boot-and-config-02 was already closed by the existing tenant-pool-budget module and I say so with measurements rather than inventing a change. The two deepest items are handled honestly: tenant-isolation-03 is fully closed (the superuser URL no longer leaves the process — a full keyspace scan of the live Redis now finds no DB credential anywhere), while tenant-isolation-02 gets a partial that is real and wired rather than an unsafe complete one — every tenant connection is now checked against the database name its tenant id must map to, so a routing bug or poisoned context throws instead of silently reading another library's data; per-tenant Postgres roles need provisioning + a control migration I do not own. reliability-17 exposed a mount-order defect I found by measuring rather than assuming: mounted in PlatformModule the middleware sat behind TenantMiddleware and counted zero of the tenant-404s the finding names, so it moved to the head of AppModule's chain and the integration test now asserts exactly that case. supply-chain-02 ships a fail-closed guard instead of a pipeline rewrite I could not exercise: today's configuration is untouched, and the first attempt to populate a signing secret fails the release with the split-pipeline design attached. Image digests are real, resolved from Docker Hub and verified to be multi-arch indexes covering linux/amd64+arm64 — none invented.

findings_addressed.what_changed: Verified closed before changing anything. apps/api/src/platform/tenant-pool-budget.ts exists AND is applied: TenantPrismaService passes plan.poolMax to every makeTenantPrismaClient call and sizes its LRU from the same plan; worker.ts computes the 'worker' plan; all five per-tenant sweeps construct `new TenantPrismaService('worker')` and tenant-pool-budget.spec.ts (9 tests) fails if one forgets. Executed the planner: shipped defaults give api peak 100 + worker peak 32 = 132 against max_connections=200 — the 250-vs-200 contradiction is gone, and a live worker /metrics scrape reported libriant_worker_tenant_conn_peak 32 / budget 42, matching. The one thing still open was that `200` was written twice with nothing keeping the copies equal, so I made compose drive both from one variable: x-app-env PG_MAX_CONNECTIONS (default 200, i.e. byte-identical behaviour when unset) and postgres `-c max_connections=${PG_MAX_CONNECTIONS:-200}`. Proved the planner tracks it: at 400 the api plan opens to 5 connections/client, at 60 it clamps down to 21x1 instead of overspending.
findings_addressed.residual_risk: tenant URLs still bypass pgbouncer and go straight to postgres:5432 (unchanged by design — pgbouncer fronts only the control DB). The planner's DEFAULT_SERVER_MAX_CONNECTIONS constant is still a literal 200; it is now only a fallback for a deployment that does not set PG_MAX_CONNECTIONS.

findings_addressed.what_changed: Both halves of the conjunction. (1) The web container healthcheck now probes /api/readyz instead of the constant /api/healthz, so the container can actually transition to unhealthy — /api/readyz already fetched ${API_INTERNAL_URL}/readyz with a 3s abort and returned 503, and no probe referenced it. /api/healthz stays as pure liveness. busybox wget exits non-zero on a 503, the same pattern the api service's own /readyz healthcheck already relies on. (2) The CI deploy gate (.github/workflows/deploy.yml 'Wait for health') now additionally curls a real page through Caddy that crosses the web→api hop: `curl --resolve $APP_HOST:443:127.0.0.1 https://$APP_HOST/api/readyz` must return 200 before the deploy is declared healthy. --resolve rather than -H so the SNI matches the origin certificate (libriant.com, *.libriant.com), which the file's own comments record as the thing that makes a healthy stack read as dead. APP_HOST comes from /srv/libriant/.env.prod (PUBLIC_HOST, defaulting to the caddy service's own app.libriant.com), sourced only if the file exists so a missing .env.prod cannot fail the gate.
findings_addressed.residual_risk: scripts/deploy-on-host.sh (the MANUAL deploy path) has the same four-signal gate and I do not own it; it now benefits from the healthcheck change but still lacks the explicit page curl. Under MAINTENANCE_HARD=true the new check gets a 200 from Caddy's static maintenance page — a false green during deliberate maintenance, never a false red.

findings_addressed.what_changed: SAY WHICH, as asked. What I did NOT do: per-tenant Postgres roles. That needs CREATE ROLE/GRANT/REVOKE in tenant-provisioning.service.ts, a writer for the already-modelled TenantDbCredential, and a control-plane migration — none of which I own, and building a reader with no writer is the 'machinery never mounted' failure. Nor did I do the audit's 'Monday-sized half' (stop persisting the password in tenants.dbUrl): the writers are tenant-provisioning.service.ts, scripts/tenant-create.ts and scripts/tenant-relocate.ts. What I DID do, entirely inside apps/api/src/tenancy/tenant-prisma*: the finding's core sentence is 'the separation between libraries is enforced only by which connection string the application picks' — that pick is now checked. assertUrlBelongsToTenant() runs on EVERY getClient() call and refuses to open a connection whose database name is not `tenant_<normalized tenant id>`, which is a pure function of the id on every path in the repo (TenantProvisioningService.dbNameFor, scripts/_lib/cli.ts dbNameForTenant, and tenant-relocate.ts which moves the HOST and keeps the name). Verified against the live control plane: 47 of 47 tenant rows satisfy the invariant, so this cannot fire on correct data. It fails closed, and the thrown message carries only the two database names — never the URL, which is a live superuser credential that would then land in the log. Six unit tests including the audit's own attack shape (tenant A's context carrying tenant B's database) and one asserting a relocate to a new host still rebuilds the client. Plus tenant-isolation-03 below removes the one copy of that credential that lived outside Postgres.
findings_addressed.residual_risk: The role is still a superuser and the password is still stored in tenants.dbUrl and therefore in every pg_dumpall backup. The new guard raises the bar for an application-level routing bug; it does nothing against anyone who already holds the connection string. The full fix remains open — see owner_actions.

findings_addressed.what_changed: The resolver no longer serialises dbUrl/storageUrl into Redis at all. The cached type is `Omit<TenantContext,'dbUrl'|'storageUrl'|'resolvedFrom'>`, so TypeScript — not vigilance — keeps a future TenantContext field from leaking in, and the two addresses live in a process-local TTL'd LRU keyed by the SAME cache key. A positive Redis hit with no local entry (another container warmed it, or we restarted) is treated as a MISS and falls through to the control-plane lookup rather than handing the middleware a context with dbUrl undefined. That key choice also makes every existing invalidation path correct for free: admin hard-delete, tenant-relocate.ts and storage-migrate.ts all DEL the Redis key directly, which forces the DB lookup that overwrites the local entry — none of them needs to learn about this cache. invalidate() clears both.
findings_addressed.residual_risk: Production Redis still runs without --requirepass. I did not ship that: it needs a new required secret in .env.prod (root-level, not mine) and compose interpolation plus a redis-cli healthcheck I cannot validate — docker is not installed on this machine, and a wrong guess there crash-loops the shipped configuration. Reported as an owner action instead. Marginal exposure is now small: the finding's own verification notes Redis is on an internal:true network with no published ports, reachable only by the api/worker that already hold PG_SUPERUSER_URL.

findings_addressed.what_changed: Dead outbox rows now have a surface. New apps/api/src/email/outbox-census.ts runs a head-count on a 60s timer (not per scrape — /metrics is synchronous and must keep working when the DB is unhappy) and the worker spreads it into /metrics. Emits libriant_email_outbox_rows{status} for EVERY EmailOutboxStatus enum value including `failed`, which the worker never writes today but which would otherwise be silently dropped from the count, and libriant_email_outbox_oldest_pending_seconds keyed on scheduledFor (a message deliberately scheduled for next week is not late). A failed pass keeps the last good snapshot rather than blanking the gauges — a gauge that vanishes during a control-DB blip would RESOLVE the dead-letter alert and make abandoned mail look cleaned up. Three alert rules in infra/monitoring/alerts.yml: LibriantEmailOutboxDeadLetters (>0), LibriantEmailOutboxStalled (oldest owed >30m), and LibriantEmailOutboxCensusMissing (absent(), so a worker that never exports is not mistaken for a quiet night). The re-drive SQL is in the dead-letter annotation, including the exception for rows whose one-time link has already expired and cannot be re-driven. Started in worker.ts rather than inside startEmailWorker so the gauges exist even when the BullMQ consumer fails to connect — exactly when the backlog matters; timer unref'd and cleared on shutdown.
findings_addressed.residual_risk: The finding's fix is a conjunction and I completed the metric+alert half only. The admin panel view with a re-drive button lives in apps/web and apps/api/src/admin, neither of which I own; the annotation's SQL is the interim operator surface. Dormant while EMAIL_DRIVER=console, as the finding says.

findings_addressed.what_changed: New apps/api/src/platform/http-metrics.ts: libriant_api_requests_total{method,route,status} and a libriant_api_request_duration_seconds histogram, rendered by health.controller.ts BEFORE the capacity block (those gauges talk to Postgres and Redis; when the DB is the broken thing the error rate is what the scrape must still carry). MOUNT POINT MATTERED AND I MEASURED IT: mounted in PlatformModule it sat behind the whole OriginCheck→Session→Admin→Impersonation→SystemMode→Tenant chain, and against a running API `/t/<unknown-slug>/members` 404'd from TenantMiddleware and produced NO series at all — losing 'a tenant whose every request errors', every maintenance 503 and every CSRF 403, i.e. the exact blind spot. It is now the FIRST entry in AppModule's configure(); it only starts a timer and registers res.on('finish'), so it cannot change any request's outcome. res.on('finish') rather than an interceptor so it also sees unmatched 404s and the status the exception filter actually sent. Route labels are Express route PATTERNS, capped at 200 distinct values; wildcard patterns fold to 'other' — Nest 11 compiles forRoutes('*') to `/{*path}`, and a label value containing braces is legal PromQL but broke my own test parser first, which is enough evidence it would break someone's dashboard. Three alert rules added: LibriantApi5xxRate (ratio, with a traffic-floor arm so one stray 500 on an idle night is not a 100% error rate), LibriantApiRouteErrors (the single broken route the fleet ratio hides), LibriantApiLatencyHigh (p95 > 2s).
findings_addressed.residual_risk: Hand-rolled rather than prom-client, deliberately (no metrics dependency exists and supply-chain-03 is in the same audit). Counters are per-process and reset on restart — correct for a counter, but a rolling deploy shows a rate discontinuity. `pnpm check:alerts` cannot run promtool; CI does that.

findings_addressed.what_changed: I did not restructure the release pipeline. A correct split means job A produces unsigned artifacts and job B re-runs electron-builder --prepackaged with the secrets, and getting the latest*.yml sha512 entries wrong after re-signing silently breaks auto-update for every desktop client — I cannot exercise GitHub Actions from here, and that failure is worse than the finding. What I shipped instead makes the latent defect impossible to trip silently. (1) Workflow-level permissions dropped from `contents: write` to `contents: read`, with write granted per job to the three that publish; `verify` now runs the whole suite with read only. (2) A fail-closed guard as the FIRST step of the release job — before checkout, before pnpm install, before any third-party code — that fails the release if MAC_CSC_LINK, APPLE_API_KEY_P8 or AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET is populated while the pipeline is still monolithic, with the split design written above it and a repository variable (DESKTOP_SIGNING_PIPELINE_SPLIT) as the explicit acknowledgement that lifts it. No secret VALUE enters that step's environment — only `secrets.X != ''` booleans. This turns the audit's 'until then, do not populate MAC_CSC_LINK / AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET' from a sentence in a document into something enforced at the moment someone adds the secret. Exercised the guard's shell in all five states: nothing set (today) passes, each secret trips it, the variable lifts it, and all-env-absent passes — so today's configuration is bit-for-bit unchanged and no deploy is blocked.
findings_addressed.residual_risk: The `release` job still runs pnpm install (four packages with arbitrary-code install hooks) in the same job that holds GITHUB_TOKEN with contents:write, which is the one live exposure the audit says remains. Narrowing that needs the split. I also did not add --ignore-scripts to the install: it would need `pnpm rebuild electron electron-winstaller` afterwards and I cannot test the Windows leg.

findings_addressed.what_changed: Not the audit's suggested fix — it says so itself: a plain `pnpm install --prod` would delete tsx, which is the API container's own entrypoint. Instead, both images now copy only the workspace manifests their runtime actually needs, because a manifest copied into the deps stage IS a dependency tree installed into the image. API image: dropped apps/web (never imported; the build stage does not even copy apps/web), packages/i18n and packages/ui (not dependencies of @libriant/api or anything it imports; sources never copied). Web image: dropped apps/api, packages/db-control and packages/db-tenant — `grep -rn 'db-control|db-tenant|@libriant/api' apps/web` returns nothing. Safety of omitting a workspace member under --frozen-lockfile is not a guess: apps/desktop is a workspace importer in the lockfile and has never been copied into ANY of the three Dockerfiles, and all three build in production today. MEASURED from the lockfile graph rather than asserted: API install closure 702→658 (44 packages, ~296 MB of node_modules — next 185 MB, @next/swc 89 MB, sharp/libvips 18 MB, and nothing else in the removed set is anything but Next/SWC/sharp); web 702→188 (514 packages, ~445 MB — @prisma/client 90 MB, @prisma/studio-core 44 MB, the Prisma CLI 44 MB, @electric-sql/pglite 23 MB, exceljs, mysql2, NestJS, Stripe). Confirmed next/react/react-dom/marked/typescript/tsx/sharp/@next/swc-linux-x64-musl all survive in the web closure, and that everything the migrate one-shot runs (db:migrate:deploy, db:seed, ingest:help→marked from the ROOT devDependencies, tenant:migrate, admin:bootstrap) is unaffected.
findings_addressed.residual_risk: Root devDependencies (turbo, eslint, prettier, typescript, tsx, marked) still ship in both images. Removing them needs tsx promoted to a runtime dependency in apps/api/package.json, which I do not own. I could not run `pnpm install` to replay the deps stage byte-for-byte (explicitly forbidden), so the package/size figures are computed from pnpm-lock.yaml reachability plus on-disk sizes in node_modules/.pnpm — the direction and the removed set are exact, the MB figures are close rather than a docker image inspect.

findings_addressed.what_changed: Every base image is now pinned tag@digest: node:26-alpine in all three Dockerfiles (apps/api, apps/web, infra/caddy), caddy:2-alpine, postgres:16-alpine, redis:8-alpine, and edoburu/pgbouncer:v1.25.2-p0 — the softest link, a single-maintainer community image sitting in the credential path with POSTGRES_PASSWORD in its environment. new_problems.issue: Moving dbUrl/storageUrl into a process-local LRU makes cross-process invalidation incomplete, and the in-code comment claims the opposite ('the ordering property this gives every EXISTING invalidation path for free … None of them needs to learn about this cache'). That reasoning holds only for a single process. tenant-relocate.ts:462 and storage-migrate.ts:287 DEL the Redis key from an EXTERNAL process; they cannot reach into a running API's memory. With two or more API processes, whichever one misses first re-warms Redis with the new identity, and any other process that still holds a live local entry then takes a positive Redis hit and merges it with its STALE dbUrl/storageUrl — routing to the old host for up to TENANT_CACHE_TTL_SEC (default 300s). Before this change the whole context lived in Redis, so a DEL was globally effective. The tenant-isolation-02 guard does NOT catch it, because relocation moves the HOST and keeps the database name, which is the only thing the guard checks. Not reachable in today's shipped topology (one `api` container, no replicas, and the worker does not use TenantResolverService), so this is latent rather than live — but it silently converts a correctness property into a deployment constraint that nothing records.
new_problems.reproduction: Scale the api service to 2 replicas. Process A serves tenant X (local addresses cached, TTL 300s). Run `pnpm tenant:relocate` for X, which moves the DB to a new host and DELs lbr:tenant:slug:X. Process B takes the next request, misses, re-reads the control DB and re-writes Redis with the new identity. Process A's next request now hits the fresh Redis entry, finds its own stale local entry, and opens a connection to the OLD host — for up to 300s, with no error, because expectedDbName() only checks the database name and the relocate preserved it.
